chapters.title: Force Is An Interaction
chapters.learningOutcome: Identify the two objects in a force interaction and distinguish contact from non-contact forces.

narration.title: Watch the motion
narration.text: Watch the two pilots on the glide track. At first, both are still. Now watch their hands. Their palms press, and both platforms begin to move apart. The motion is our first clue. Which two objects are interacting?

narration.title: A force needs two
narration.text: A force is a push or pull during an interaction. The blue pilot pushes on the orange pilot. At the same moment, the orange pilot pushes on the blue pilot. One interaction produces two forces, acting on two different objects.

narration.title: Name both objects
narration.text: Follow each arrow to the object receiving the push. Blue on orange belongs with the orange pilot. Orange on blue belongs with the blue pilot. The arrows are equal in length and point in opposite directions. One interaction; two force arrows.

narration.title: Motion is evidence
narration.text: Compare the evidence before and after contact. Before the push, both platforms are still. Afterwards, they move apart. The change is motion. We do not see a force floating through the air; we identify the interaction and measure what changes.

narration.title: The push has ended
narration.text: Here is an idea worth testing: perhaps the push travels inside each pilot. Check the sequence. While their palms touch, the contact-force arrows are present. When their hands separate, those arrows disappear. The platforms keep gliding, but that contact push has ended.

narration.title: Push or pull
narration.text: Contact forces can push or pull. In the first bay, the robot's padded hand pushes the cart. In the second, the robot pulls the trolley through a taut cable. In both cases, name the pair. One object alone cannot describe an interaction.

narration.title: No touch required
narration.text: Now focus on the gap between the magnets. They do not touch, yet both carts can begin to move. That is evidence of a non-contact interaction. Gravity is another example: Earth pulls objects towards it without making surface contact.

narration.title: Contact or non-contact
narration.text: Use two questions to classify an interaction. First: which two objects are involved? Second: do they touch? A robot hand on a cart is contact. Magnet on magnet is non-contact. Earth pulling an object is non-contact. Strength does not choose the label; touching does.

narration.title: Test one change
narration.text: For a fair comparison, keep the cart, track, and starting line the same. Change only the size of the push, then measure the distance travelled in the same time. If several conditions change together, the evidence cannot tell us which change mattered.

narration.title: Repair the explanation
narration.text: Return to the pilots. Their platforms are still moving after their hands separate. Does that mean a push is stored inside them? No. The contact interaction happened first and changed their motion. After contact ends, the new motion can continue while other forces still act.

narration.title: Predict the evidence
narration.text: Make a prediction before the magnet trial runs. Which observations would support a non-contact interaction? Take three quiet seconds to decide. Now check: the gap remains visible, both carts change motion, and no hand touches either cart. Those observations support the claim.

narration.title: Your physics move
narration.text: Use this physicist's routine whenever you investigate a force. Name both objects. Decide whether they touch. Then use a change in motion as evidence. A force is not hidden material carried by one object. A force belongs to an interaction between objects.

tests.prompt: Two skaters press palms and move apart. Which statement names the interaction most completely?
options: Skater A pushes skater B, and skater B pushes skater A
The floor gives both skaters stored motion
tests.feedback: A force interaction involves two objects. Each skater pushes on the other during contact.

tests.prompt: A foot kicks a still ball. Which object pair belongs in the contact-force explanation?
tests.feedback: The foot and ball touch during the kick, so they are the relevant interaction pair.

tests.prompt: Skater A is on the left and pushes Skater B to the right. Which way should the arrow labelled 'A on B' point?
tests.feedback: The arrow shows the direction of the force on B, so it points to the right.

tests.prompt: A hand pulls a trolley left with a rope. Which arrow best represents 'rope on trolley'?
options: An arrow left from the trolley
An arrow right from the trolley
An arrow down from the rope
No arrow because pulling is not a force
tests.feedback: The rope pulls the trolley left, so the force arrow on the trolley points left.

tests.prompt: Both skaters are still before their palms meet and moving apart afterwards. What is the strongest evidence that forces acted?
options: Their motion changed after the contact
tests.feedback: A change from still to moving is observable evidence that forces affected the skaters' motion.

tests.prompt: A cart is still, then speeds up while a hand pushes it. Which two observations form useful before-and-after evidence?
options: Still before and speeding up during the push
tests.feedback: Comparing motion before and during the push links the interaction to a visible change.

tests.prompt: The skaters' hands separate, but they continue gliding. What happened to the hand-to-hand push?
tests.feedback: The hand-to-hand contact force ends when the hands separate; continuing motion does not mean the push is stored.

tests.prompt: A foot leaves a kicked ball. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: The foot's push continues inside the ball
The foot-ball force ended when contact ended
No force acted at any time
The ball now creates its own kick
tests.feedback: The foot's contact force acts during contact and ends when the foot leaves the ball.

tests.prompt: Two magnet carts begin still with a visible gap and then move apart. Which conclusion fits the evidence?
options: A contact push acted through the track
A non-contact magnetic interaction changed their motion
The carts stored force before the test
No force acted because they did not touch
tests.feedback: The gap remains visible while motion changes, supporting a non-contact magnetic interaction.

tests.prompt: A book falls after being released. Which interaction can act without contact between the book and the ground?
tests.feedback: Earth's gravitational pull on the book is a non-contact interaction.

tests.prompt: A rope moves a trolley towards a child. Which description is complete?
options: The rope pulls on the trolley during contact
The child stores force in the trolley
Gravity pulls the trolley towards the child
tests.feedback: The rope and trolley interact through contact, and the rope pulls the trolley.

tests.prompt: A hand moves a cart away from the child. Which words best describe the interaction?
tests.feedback: The hand is in contact with the cart and pushes it away.

tests.prompt: A student compares a gentle and strong push. Which plan gives the clearest evidence?
options: Change the cart, surface and push together
Use the same cart and surface, change only the push, and measure distance
Use two carts and guess which moved faster
Change only the surface and call it a push test
tests.feedback: Keeping the cart and surface the same isolates the push as the changed variable.

tests.prompt: Two carts travel different distances, but one ran on carpet and one on tile. Why can this test not compare push strength fairly?
options: A strong push never changes motion
tests.feedback: Changing the surface as well as the push creates two possible causes for the distance difference.

tests.prompt: Which claim contains the 'force is stored inside' misconception?
options: A hand pushes a cart during contact
A magnet can push another magnet across a gap
The kick's force rides inside the ball after contact
Earth pulls on a falling book
tests.feedback: A force is an interaction; the foot-ball contact force does not ride inside the ball.

tests.prompt: A student says, 'No force can act unless objects touch.' Which observation best challenges the claim?
tests.feedback: The visible gap and changing motion show that a magnetic force can act without contact.

tests.prompt: A ball changes from still to moving when kicked. Which reasoning chain is strongest?
options: The ball moved, so it must contain force
Foot and ball touched; the foot pushed the ball; the ball's motion changed
The goal pulled the ball forwards
The ball moved because moving is natural
tests.feedback: The answer names the interacting objects, the push and the observed change in motion.

tests.prompt: Two magnets do not touch, yet one cart starts moving. Which three-part explanation is best?
options: There was a gap; magnetic interaction acted; motion changed
The cart had wheels; wheels contain force; motion appeared
The bench pushed sideways; the magnet did nothing
tests.feedback: The explanation links the visible gap, a non-contact interaction and the change in motion.

tests.prompt: A diagram shows only one arrow labelled 'push' between two skaters. What is the most useful improvement?
options: Add the two object names and show the matching opposite interaction
Remove all arrows because forces are invisible
tests.feedback: Object-pair labels and the matching interaction make the force model precise.

tests.prompt: Which final explanation uses claim and evidence most effectively?
options: A force happened because I think so
The magnets repelled because they are blue
A non-contact magnetic push acted because the carts moved apart while a gap remained
The carts moved because the track was long
tests.feedback: The claim names the force type and the evidence identifies the visible gap and motion change.

chapters.title: Motion Tells The Story
chapters.learningOutcome: Use before-and-after evidence to explain changes in motion.

narration.title: Three tracks, one mystery
narration.text: Three identical balls. Three different tracks. Each ball gets the same launch. Tile, short grass, or thick carpet: which ball will travel furthest before it stops? Make your prediction, then watch for evidence.

narration.title: Run the comparison
narration.text: All three begin still. The same launcher setting sends each ball across a smooth launch strip. A timing gate confirms the same entry speed before each test surface. Now the launcher is clear. Tile gives the longest stopping distance. Grass is shorter. Carpet is shortest.

narration.title: Name the motion changes
narration.text: Motion can tell several stories. Still to moving means start. More distance in the same time means speed up. Less distance each moment means slow down. No new distance means stop. A new path means change direction.

narration.title: Before and after evidence
narration.text: A physicist compares before and after. Before the launch, the carpet ball is still. Just after contact, it is moving. Later, its gaps become smaller. Finally, its position no longer changes. That sequence is measurable evidence.

narration.title: The kick has ended
narration.text: Look closely at the contact. While the launcher touches the ball, launcher on ball is a forward push. Once the launcher separates, that contact force ends. The ball can still be moving even though the kick is over.

narration.title: What slows the ball?
narration.text: The moving ball still interacts with its surroundings. The surface touches the ball. In this carpet model, friction and carpet deformation produce a backward surface resistance. The greater slowing effect gives a shorter stopping distance.

narration.title: Build a fair test
narration.text: To compare surfaces fairly, keep the ball, entry speed, and start line the same. Change only the surface. Measure from the surface start to the resting ball. Repeat each run, because one surprising run may not represent the pattern.

narration.title: Read the data
narration.text: Check all three runs before the averages. Tile measures three hundred and thirty-five, three hundred and forty-five, and three hundred and forty centimetres: average three hundred and forty. Grass averages two hundred and twenty. Carpet averages one hundred and ten. The graph and tracks show the same pattern.

narration.title: Test the tempting idea
narration.text: A tempting explanation says the kick force rides inside the ball and slowly runs out. But the contact arrow ended when the launcher separated. The remaining evidence shows a ball moving while surface friction acts against that motion. The kick is not stored inside.

narration.title: Direction is evidence too
narration.text: A force can change direction as well as speed. A rolling ball meets an angled bumper. The bumper-on-ball force points away from the bumper surface. That force changes the ball's motion into a new path: straight in, diagonal out.

narration.title: Make a prediction
narration.text: Suppose we replace thick carpet with a more deformable, higher-resistance rubber mat while everything else stays the same. Predict the stopping distance. Would it be longer than tile, between tile and carpet, or shorter than carpet? Use the model, then test it. Our testable prediction is shorter than carpet.

narration.title: Your evidence routine
narration.text: Use this motion routine. Compare before and after. Name the motion change. Name the interacting objects. Then connect the force to visible evidence. The ball does not carry a used-up kick. Motion changes because objects are interacting now, or interacted earlier while other forces continue to act.

tests.prompt: A ball is still, then rolls after a launcher touches it. Which motion change occurred?
tests.feedback: The before-and-after evidence changes from still to moving, so the ball started.

tests.prompt: A cart keeps the same speed, hits a bumper, then moves diagonally. What changed?
tests.feedback: The path before and after contact shows a change in direction.

tests.prompt: Position dots become closer together each second. What does that show?
tests.feedback: Smaller distances in equal times show that the object is slowing down.

tests.prompt: Position dots become farther apart each second. Which conclusion fits?
tests.feedback: Larger distances in equal time intervals show increasing speed.

tests.prompt: When does the launcher's contact force on the ball end?
tests.feedback: The launcher-on-ball contact force ends when contact ends.

tests.prompt: A foot leaves a kicked ball, but the ball keeps moving. Which statement is accurate?
options: The foot-ball push ended at separation
The ball now has no interactions
tests.feedback: Continuing motion does not mean the earlier contact force is stored.

tests.prompt: In this carpet model, a ball rolls right while carpet deforms beneath it. Which arrow represents the net surface resistance?
options: A left arrow on the ball
A right arrow on the ball
A downward arrow on the start gate
A forward launcher arrow after separation
tests.feedback: For this model, the friction-and-deformation effect is represented by a backward surface-resistance arrow.

tests.prompt: Which two objects form the surface interaction that slows a ball on grass?
tests.feedback: The touching ball and grass are the relevant surface interaction pair.

tests.prompt: Same ball and entry speed: tile 340 cm, grass 220 cm, carpet 110 cm. Which stops after the shortest distance?
options: The data shows only stopping time
tests.feedback: The carpet run has the shortest measured stopping distance.

tests.prompt: Which observation best supports a greater slowing effect on carpet than tile?
options: The ball stops after a shorter distance on carpet
The carpet trial begins at a different speed
The tile trial runs for less time
The carpet ball has greater mass
tests.feedback: With entry speed and ball controlled, stopping distance is relevant motion evidence.

tests.prompt: Which plan fairly compares tile and carpet?
options: Same ball and launch; change only surface; repeat and measure
tests.feedback: A fair surface test holds the ball, launch and start constant, then repeats measurements.

tests.prompt: One trial uses a small ball entering tile at 1 m/s and a large ball entering carpet at 2 m/s. Why is the comparison weak?
options: Ball and entry speed both changed
Stopping distance is the controlled variable
tests.feedback: Changing ball and entry speed prevents a clear conclusion about the surface.

tests.prompt: Which order matches the measured stopping distances from longest to shortest?
tests.feedback: The data is tile 340 cm, grass 220 cm, carpet 110 cm.

tests.prompt: Tile runs measure 335, 345 and 340 cm. Why is 340 cm a useful summary?
options: It is the average of the repeated runs
It proves every future run is 340
tests.feedback: The average summarises the three close repeated measurements without claiming every run is identical.

tests.prompt: Which sentence contains the stored-kick misconception?
options: The kick ended when contact ended
Surface friction acts while the ball rolls
Kick force rides inside the ball and runs out
The ball's motion can be measured
tests.feedback: A force belongs to an interaction; the kick does not ride inside the ball.

tests.prompt: Which evidence most directly challenges 'the kick stays inside the ball'?
options: The contact arrow disappears at separation while the ball keeps moving
tests.feedback: The force arrow ends with contact, separating the earlier push from later motion.

tests.prompt: A ball hits an angled bumper and turns. Which force arrow is most defensible?
options: Bumper on ball pointing away from the bumper surface
A motion arrow labelled force along the old path
Launcher on ball after contact has ended
A friction arrow pointing through the bumper
tests.feedback: The bumper's contact force points away from its surface and changes the ball's velocity.

tests.prompt: Which before-and-after evidence best shows a direction change?
options: Straight path in, diagonal path out
Blue ball in, blue ball out
tests.feedback: A changed path is direct evidence of changed direction.

tests.prompt: Which explanation best uses claim and evidence?
options: Carpet slowed the ball more because its stopping distance was shortest in repeated fair runs
Carpet wins because it looks thick
The kick ran out first on carpet
tests.feedback: The explanation links a force claim to repeated stopping-distance evidence.

tests.prompt: A higher-resistance mat gives repeated stopping distances shorter than carpet at the same entry speed. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The mat produced a greater slowing effect in this fair test
All rubber mats always stop every object fastest
The launcher force ran out inside the ball
The shorter distance proves the ball entered more slowly
tests.feedback: The claim stays within the fair test and links the measured pattern to the changed surface.

chapters.title: Push, Pull And Support
chapters.learningOutcome: Model applied and support forces with a comparison meter.

narration.title: The quiet force mystery
narration.text: This book is not moving, but the foam beneath it is squashed. Is the foam doing nothing? Watch the contact patch. The book presses down, and the foam changes shape. What might the foam be doing to the book?

narration.title: Name both objects
narration.text: The book and foam interact through contact. Book on foam pushes down; foam on book pushes up. Those arrows act on different objects. To explain the resting book, follow forces on the book: Earth on book points down, while foam on book support points up.

narration.title: Still can have forces
narration.text: The book remains still while the foam is supporting it. Remove the foam, and the book begins to fall. Put the support back, and the book can rest again. Stillness is not proof that no forces act.

narration.title: Change the load
narration.text: Add a second identical book. The foam squashes further. To support the resting stack, the foam's upward push is greater than it was for one book. A longer arrow shows greater force within this comparison.

narration.title: Applied pushes
narration.text: Now move to the cart. A robot hand touches the cart and pushes to the right. Hand on cart is an applied force. The arrow begins on the cart and points in the direction of the push.

narration.title: Applied pulls
narration.text: A rubber band can pull the same cart. The band stretches towards the robot. Rubber band on cart points towards the robot too. Push and pull describe the direction of the applied interaction; neither is material stored in the cart.

narration.title: Build a comparison meter
narration.text: We can use band stretch as a comparison meter. Mark the resting length as zero centimetres. Then read how many centimetres the band stretches while pulling. More stretch means a greater pull in this investigation. These are relative readings, not Newtons.

narration.title: Run a fair pull test
narration.text: Keep the cart, surface, and start line the same. First, hold a two-centimetre stretch for one second. Reset. Then hold a four-centimetre stretch for one second. Change only the stretch reading and measure the distance after the same time.

narration.title: Read the result
narration.text: At two centimetres, the cart travels eighty centimetres. At four centimetres, it travels one hundred and fifty centimetres. The larger stretch reading goes with the larger change in motion in this test. The data supports a stronger-pull explanation.

narration.title: Repair the silent-table idea
narration.text: Now test the claim: a table does nothing because it does not move. Place the foam and book on the table. The contact patch changes shape, and the book rests instead of passing through. The surface is part of the interaction.

narration.title: Choose the correct model
narration.text: Which model fits the forces acting on a book resting on foam? One downward Earth-on-book arrow only? No arrows because it is still? Or Earth on book down paired with foam on book support up? Choose, then check the contact evidence.

narration.title: Your force-model routine
narration.text: Use this routine. Name both objects. Mark the contact. Draw the force on the receiving object. Point the arrow in the force direction. When comparing pulls, use the same meter and a fair test. Even a still surface can push. Evidence makes that invisible interaction understandable.

tests.prompt: A book rests on squashed foam. Which objects form the support interaction?
tests.feedback: The touching book and foam are the interaction pair.

tests.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the book-foam interaction pair?
options: Book pushes foam down and foam pushes book up
Both arrows act on the book
Only the book exerts a force
Earth and table are the contact pair
tests.feedback: The two contact forces act on different receivers: one on foam and one on book.

tests.prompt: Which way should the arrow labelled 'foam on book' point?
tests.feedback: The foam's support force on the book points upward.

tests.prompt: Where should a support-force arrow be anchored in the book-and-foam model?
tests.feedback: A force arrow is drawn on the object receiving the force.

tests.prompt: A book is still on a table. Which forces-on-book model is best?
options: Earth on book down and table on book up
No forces because it is still
Book on table down is the only force on the book
tests.feedback: The book can remain still while Earth pulls down and the table supports it upward.

tests.prompt: Which observation challenges 'the foam does nothing'?
options: The foam compresses where the book touches
tests.feedback: Visible compression is evidence that the foam is part of the contact interaction.

tests.prompt: A second identical book is added and the foam compresses further. What should happen to the support arrow in this comparison?
tests.feedback: For the resting stack, greater compression is modelled with a greater upward support force.

tests.prompt: What does a longer upward support arrow mean within the one-book versus two-book scene?
options: Greater support force in this comparison
The arrow acts on the foam
tests.feedback: Within the same comparison, arrow length represents relative force strength on the receiving stack.

tests.prompt: A robot hand pushes a cart right. Which arrow is correct?
options: Cart on hand pointing right from empty space
No arrow because the cart moves
tests.feedback: The applied force on the receiving cart points in the push direction.

tests.prompt: Which two objects belong in the applied-push label?
tests.feedback: The hand and cart touch during the applied push.

tests.prompt: A stretched rubber band pulls a cart towards a robot. Which way does 'band on cart' point?
tests.feedback: The pull on the cart points along the stretched band towards the robot.

tests.prompt: Which sentence correctly separates pull from later motion?
options: The stretched band pulls during contact; that pull ends when the band disconnects
The cart carries the band's pull after disconnection
The pull becomes the cart's speed
The cart pulls itself after release
tests.feedback: A pull is an interaction; later motion is not stored pull material.

tests.prompt: In this comparison meter, what does 4 cm of stretch mean compared with 2 cm?
options: A greater pull in this investigation
The cart is twice as heavy
tests.feedback: More stretch represents a greater relative pull here; centimetres are not Newtons.

tests.prompt: Why must the meter be labelled 'relative comparison'?
options: Centimetres measure stretch, not a standard force unit
tests.feedback: The ruler measures band stretch as a proxy for comparing pulls, not force in Newtons.

tests.prompt: Which plan fairly compares 2 cm and 4 cm stretches?
options: Same cart, surface, start and time; change only stretch
tests.feedback: Holding other conditions constant isolates the stretch reading.

tests.prompt: Why is a 2 cm pull for one second versus a 4 cm pull for three seconds unfair?
tests.feedback: Changing both stretch and pull time creates two possible causes.

tests.prompt: The cart travels 80 cm at 2 cm stretch and 150 cm at 4 cm stretch. What does the data support?
options: The larger stretch went with a larger motion change
tests.feedback: The fair-test data links the larger relative pull with greater distance in the same time.

tests.prompt: Which graph matches the fair pull test?
options: A 150 cm bar for 4 cm stretch and 80 cm bar for 2 cm
A 150 cm bar for 2 cm and 80 cm for 4 cm
Equal bars because the same cart was used
Bars of stretch rather than measured cart distance
tests.feedback: The 4 cm trial produced the greater measured cart distance.

tests.prompt: Which is the strongest forces-on-book model for a book resting on foam?
options: Earth on book down and foam on book up, both anchored to the book
Book on foam down and foam on book up as if both act on the book
No arrows because the book is still
tests.feedback: A forces-on-one-object model keeps both arrows on the receiving book and names both source objects.

tests.prompt: Which explanation fully names the pair, direction and evidence?
options: Foam pushes upward on the book; the compressed contact patch and resting book support that model
The foam has force because it is blue
The book pushes down, so that is the only force on the book
The table is still, so no upward interaction exists
tests.feedback: The answer identifies source and receiver, upward direction, and relevant contact evidence.

chapters.title: Friction Grips
chapters.learningOutcome: Explain how friction can help or hinder motion.

narration.title: Which shoe will grip?
narration.text: Two identical shoes meet two surfaces: smooth ice and rough bitumen. The same sideways push will act on each shoe. Which one will slide farther? Lock in your prediction, then watch the contact patches instead of the shoe tops.

narration.title: Watch the contact
narration.text: The shoe on ice slips a long way. The shoe on bitumen grips and stops quickly. Between each shoe and surface, friction acts against the slipping. Here, stronger friction helps the shoe hold its position.

narration.title: Same cart, new job
narration.text: Now the same cart enters tile and a textured mat at the same speed. It rolls farther on tile and stops sooner on the mat. This time friction hinders the cart's motion. The same force can help one job and hinder another.

narration.title: Model the surface force
narration.text: Zoom into the wheel touching the mat. The orange arrow is labelled mat on cart and points opposite the cart's sliding direction. Friction is a contact force between touching surfaces; it is not a force stored inside either object.

narration.title: Help or hinder?
narration.text: Compare the jobs. A runner needs shoe-ground friction to push without slipping. A cart designed to coast needs less friction slowing its wheels. Do not label friction good or bad. Ask whether it helps or hinders the intended motion.

narration.title: Read the stopping evidence
narration.text: Three tile runs stop at 338, 342 and 340 centimetres. Three mat runs stop at 118, 122 and 120 centimetres. The shorter repeated distances show a greater slowing effect on the mat in this investigation.

narration.title: Build a fair comparison
narration.text: To compare surfaces fairly, keep the cart, wheels, start line and entry speed the same. Change only the surface. Measure stopping distance from the entry line, reset carefully, and repeat each surface three times.

narration.title: Spot the unfair trial
narration.text: One trial uses a heavy cart pushed hard on tile and a light cart pushed gently on carpet. That cannot isolate the surface. More than one condition changed, so either the cart, the push or the surface could explain the result.

narration.title: Design for the job
narration.text: A bicycle needs friction at the brake pads and tyres so it can slow and grip the road. It also uses smooth, well-aligned wheel parts to reduce unwanted friction. Good design increases friction where grip is needed and reduces it where motion should stay easy.

narration.title: Test the tempting claim
narration.text: Someone claims, friction is always bad because it wastes motion. Test that claim with the runner. Remove most shoe-ground friction and the foot slides backward. The runner cannot push safely. The evidence does not support the claim.

narration.title: Use purpose and evidence
narration.text: Replace the claim with a stronger one: friction can help or hinder, depending on the job. Use evidence, not surface appearance alone. Stopping distance shows slowing; slipping shows lost grip; repeated fair trials make either conclusion more trustworthy.

narration.title: Choose the better sole
narration.text: A designer tests two shoe soles on the same wet path with the same load and push. Sole A slips 70 centimetres; Sole B slips 24. Which sole gives more useful friction, and which measurements justify your choice?

tests.prompt: A shoe slides right across a path. Which friction-force model is best?
options: Shoe on path pointing left, drawn on the shoe
A right arrow stored inside the shoe
tests.feedback: Friction from the path acts on the sliding shoe opposite its rightward slip.

tests.prompt: Which objects form the friction interaction while a cart wheel slides on a mat?
tests.feedback: Friction is a contact interaction between the touching wheel and mat, not an earlier push or a different force pair.

tests.prompt: Why is shoe-ground friction useful to a runner?
options: It helps the foot grip instead of sliding backward
It stores speed inside the shoe
tests.feedback: Grip lets the runner push against the ground without the foot slipping backward.

tests.prompt: Which example shows friction helping the intended job?
options: Brake pads slowing a bicycle wheel
A rusty axle resisting every turn
A box dragging when it should slide easily
A toy car stopping before the finish
tests.feedback: Brake friction is useful because the intended job is to slow the wheel.

tests.prompt: A cart is meant to coast far. How can friction hinder that job?
options: It acts against the cart's sliding and shortens its travel
It pulls the cart towards Earth
It keeps the launch push inside the cart
tests.feedback: Friction opposing the motion can make the cart slow and stop sooner.

tests.prompt: Which statement about friction is most accurate?
options: It can help grip or hinder motion, depending on the job
It always makes objects move faster
tests.feedback: The effect may be useful or unwanted; the intended job determines which.

tests.prompt: The same cart enters tile and mat at the same speed. It stops sooner on the mat. What does this support?
options: The mat produced a greater slowing effect in this test
The cart was heavier on the mat
The launch force ran out sooner
tests.feedback: With entry speed and cart controlled, the shorter stopping distance supports a greater surface slowing effect.

tests.prompt: Tile stops are 338, 342 and 340 cm; mat stops are 118, 122 and 120 cm. Which conclusion fits the data?
options: The cart repeatedly travelled farther on tile
Every run on both surfaces was identical
The mat gave the cart a larger launch
tests.feedback: All three tile distances are much longer than all three mat distances.

tests.prompt: In a fair surface test, which condition should change?
tests.feedback: Changing only the surface lets the stopping-distance difference be linked to surface interaction.

tests.prompt: What should be measured to compare how strongly each surface slows the cart?
options: Stopping distance from the entry line
tests.feedback: Stopping distance is the outcome being compared; entry speed, wheel size and cart mass should be controlled.

tests.prompt: Which plan is the fairest comparison of tile and carpet?
options: Same cart, wheels and entry speed; change only surface
Same surface but different start lines
One gentle tile run and one hard carpet run
tests.feedback: The controlled cart and entry speed isolate the surface as the changed condition.

tests.prompt: Why is a heavy cart pushed hard on tile versus a light cart pushed gently on carpet unfair?
options: Cart, push and surface all changed
tests.feedback: Several changes create several possible causes, so the surface effect cannot be isolated.

tests.prompt: Why repeat each stopping-distance trial three times?
options: To see whether the pattern is consistent
To make the cart permanently faster
tests.feedback: Repeated measurements reveal variation and make a consistent pattern more trustworthy.

tests.prompt: One mat run is 210 cm, but two others are 119 and 121 cm. What is the best next step?
options: Check the unusual run and repeat carefully
Use only 210 because it is largest
Conclude the surface has no effect
tests.feedback: The unusual result should be checked rather than selected or ignored without investigation.

tests.prompt: A cart rolls right while friction slows it. Where should the friction arrow be drawn?
options: On the finish sign, pointing down
tests.feedback: A force-on-cart arrow belongs on the receiving cart and points opposite the sliding.

tests.prompt: Which label fully names the friction force acting on a shoe?
tests.feedback: The label names the source object, path, and the receiving object, shoe.

tests.prompt: Which claim is the misconception tested in this chapter?
tests.feedback: Friction can provide useful grip as well as unwanted resistance, so it is not always bad.

tests.prompt: Which evidence most directly challenges 'friction is always bad'?
options: A low-friction shoe slides and the runner cannot push safely
tests.feedback: The runner needs shoe-ground friction for safe grip, directly showing a useful effect.

tests.prompt: Sole A slips 70 cm and Sole B slips 24 cm in repeated fair wet-path tests. Which design choice is strongest?
options: Choose B for greater useful grip, supported by its shorter slips
Choose A because longer is always better
Choose by colour because distance is irrelevant
tests.feedback: For a grip task, consistently shorter slip distances support choosing Sole B.

tests.prompt: A scooter needs grip at its tyre but easy turning at its axle. Which design uses friction wisely?
options: Increase tyre grip and reduce unwanted axle friction
Change the rider instead of testing parts
tests.feedback: The design matches friction to two different jobs: grip at the tyre and easy movement at the axle.

chapters.title: Gravity Pulls
chapters.learningOutcome: Explain Earth's non-contact pull on objects.

narration.title: Ball or feather?
narration.text: A ball and feather wait at the same height. In ordinary air, which reaches the floor first? Make a prediction, but also predict why. We will change the air without changing the objects, height or release time.

narration.title: Watch the open-air drop
narration.text: Release. The ball lands first while the feather drifts. That observation is real, but it does not prove gravity pulls only on the ball. Another interaction is affecting the feather. Watch the air bend and flow around it.

narration.title: Remove one interaction
narration.text: Seal both objects inside a clear chamber and remove almost all the air, creating a vacuum. The starting height and release stay the same. If gravity needs air, neither object should fall. If air caused the difference, what should happen?

narration.title: Model Earth's pull
narration.text: Gravity is Earth's pull on each object without direct contact. Draw a violet Earth on ball arrow downward on the ball, and Earth on feather downward on the feather. Both arrows remain whether the chamber contains air or not.

narration.title: Add the air interaction
narration.text: In open air, moving air particles touch the falling objects. Air resistance acts against their downward motion. Its effect is much more noticeable on the wide, light feather, so the feather falls more slowly even while gravity still pulls it downward.

narration.title: Run the chamber test
narration.text: Release them in the vacuum. Ball and feather fall together and land together. Gravity did not disappear when the air was removed. Removing most air resistance removed the large difference between their motions. Hold that result and compare both landing frames.

narration.title: Which way does gravity pull?
narration.text: Zoom out to Earth. Objects above Australia, Africa and the Pacific each have an Earth-on-object arrow pointing towards Earth's centre. Down means towards the ground beneath you because Earth pulls objects towards its centre from every side.

narration.title: Protect the comparison
narration.text: A strong comparison uses the same ball, feather, chamber, starting heights and release time. The air condition is the planned change. Compare landing times, repeat the drops, and do not secretly change the feather's shape between trials.

narration.title: What if something floats?
narration.text: A helium balloon can rise, yet Earth still pulls it downward. The surrounding air pushes upward strongly enough for the motion to be upward. Rising or floating describes the motion; it does not mean gravity has switched off.

narration.title: Test gravity needs air
narration.text: Someone claims gravity needs air to work. The vacuum result rejects that idea: with almost no air resistance, both objects still speed downward and land. The changed air condition affected their difference, not the existence of Earth's pull.

narration.title: Separate the two forces
narration.text: Use two questions. Is Earth pulling the object? Yes, near Earth's surface. Is air resistance affecting its fall? Only when air touches the moving object. Keeping these interactions separate explains both the open-air result and the vacuum result.

narration.title: Predict a paper test
narration.text: A flat sheet and a tightly crumpled sheet use the same paper. In air, the flat sheet falls more slowly. In a vacuum, what should change, and which force remains on both sheets? Use the two-force model to justify your answer.

tests.prompt: Which objects form the gravity interaction for a falling ball near the ground?
tests.feedback: Gravity is the non-contact interaction between Earth and the ball; the other pairs describe different or absent contacts.

tests.prompt: Which statement best describes gravity near Earth's surface?
options: Earth pulls objects without direct contact
Gravity is made by the floor
tests.feedback: Earth exerts a non-contact pull on nearby objects whether they are moving or still.

tests.prompt: Which way should an 'Earth on ball' arrow point for a ball above the ground?
tests.feedback: Earth's gravitational pull on the ball points towards Earth's centre.

tests.prompt: A ball is held still in a hand. Where is its gravity arrow?
options: On the ball, pointing towards Earth's centre
On Earth, pointing away from the ball
Missing because the ball is still
tests.feedback: The force-on-ball model keeps Earth's pull on the receiving ball even while it is held still.

tests.prompt: Why does a feather usually fall more slowly than a ball in air?
options: Air resistance has a more noticeable effect on the feather
tests.feedback: Air touching the moving feather strongly affects its motion while gravity still acts downward.

tests.prompt: Which force acts against the downward motion of a falling object in air?
tests.feedback: Air resistance is a contact force from air that opposes motion through it.

tests.prompt: A ball and feather land together in a vacuum. What does this show?
options: Gravity still acts when almost all air is removed
No forces acted during the fall
tests.feedback: Both objects falling in the near-absence of air shows that gravity does not require air.

tests.prompt: What changed between the open-air and vacuum chamber drops?
tests.feedback: The chamber comparison changes the air condition while keeping the objects and release setup the same.

tests.prompt: Which plan fairly compares a ball and feather in air and vacuum?
options: Same objects, heights and release time; change only the air condition
Drop the ball first and feather later
Change object shape and air together
tests.feedback: Controlling the setup isolates the effect of changing the air condition.

tests.prompt: Why should the feather keep the same shape in both chamber trials?
options: Changing shape could also change air resistance
Only starting height can affect a fall
A vacuum makes shape irrelevant to a fair comparison
tests.feedback: Keeping shape constant avoids adding another possible cause for changed motion.

tests.prompt: A helium balloon rises. Which explanation is best?
options: Earth still pulls down while the surrounding air pushes upward more strongly
The balloon contains stored upward motion
tests.feedback: Upward motion does not remove gravity; another force can have the greater effect on motion.

tests.prompt: An object floats without moving up or down. What can you conclude about gravity?
options: Gravity may still act while another interaction supports the object
No forces can act on a still object
tests.feedback: Stillness or floating does not mean Earth's gravitational pull has disappeared.

tests.prompt: Which observation directly rejects 'gravity needs air'?
options: Objects still fall inside a vacuum chamber
The chamber has a glass wall
A ball rolls on a table
tests.feedback: Falling continues when almost all air is removed, so air is not required for gravity.

tests.prompt: Which claim confuses gravity with air resistance?
options: The feather falls slowly because gravity barely acts on it
Earth pulls both ball and feather
tests.feedback: The feather's slower open-air fall comes from air resistance, not gravity nearly disappearing.

tests.prompt: Where should gravity arrows point for objects at different places around Earth?
options: All towards the top of the page
tests.feedback: Gravity points towards Earth's centre, so page direction changes with location around the globe.

tests.prompt: An object moves sideways after being thrown. Which gravity arrow is correct?
options: Earth on object towards Earth's centre
No arrow until the object falls straight
tests.feedback: Earth's pull remains directed towards Earth's centre even when the object's motion is sideways.

tests.prompt: A flat paper sheet and crumpled sheet fall differently in air. What is the safest conclusion?
options: Their shapes cause air to affect their motion differently
Gravity acts only on the crumpled sheet
The flat sheet has no Earth interaction
The crumpled sheet stores more falling force
tests.feedback: With the same paper, shape changes how air resistance affects the fall.

tests.prompt: What should happen to the same flat and crumpled paper in a vacuum?
options: Their falling motions should become much more alike
Only the crumpled sheet should feel gravity
tests.feedback: Removing most air resistance removes the main reason their open-air falls differ.

tests.prompt: Which explanation uses both the open-air and vacuum evidence?
options: Earth pulls both objects; air resistance makes the feather lag in air, but not in vacuum
Gravity turns on only after the chamber is sealed
The ball carries more stored downward force
tests.feedback: The explanation keeps gravity present and uses the changed air interaction to explain the different results.

tests.prompt: A designer wants to test how air changes a paper drop. Which evidence plan is strongest?
options: Repeat matched drops with the same paper and release setup under two air conditions
Compare unrelated videos with different papers
Change paper, height and air at once
Use one drop and choose the expected result
tests.feedback: Matched repeated trials isolate the air condition and produce evidence that can support a careful conclusion.

chapters.title: Magnets Push And Pull
chapters.learningOutcome: Predict magnetic attraction and repulsion using evidence.

narration.title: Which objects will move?
narration.text: A steel paperclip, aluminium strip, copper wire and wooden bead sit behind a clear line. A bar magnet approaches without touching. Which objects will move? Choose before the magnet crosses the distance markers, and do not use shiny as your rule.

narration.title: Test across a gap
narration.text: The steel paperclip moves across the gap. In this test, the aluminium, copper and wood do not. Magnetic force can act without contact, but magnets do not attract every metal. Material evidence matters more than colour or shine.

narration.title: Check the material pattern
narration.text: Reset each object at the same two-centimetre gap and repeat three times. Steel responds each time; the others show no visible movement. The repeated pattern supports a careful claim about these tested materials, not every object in the world.

narration.title: Meet the two poles
narration.text: A bar magnet has two poles, marked north in red and south in blue. Keep those colours and labels fixed. Bring a north pole near a south pole, leaving a visible gap so the non-contact interaction is easy to see.

narration.title: Opposite poles attract
narration.text: Release. The magnets move together. Attraction means the magnetic forces pull the magnets towards each other. Draw magenta arrows on both receiving magnets, each pointing towards the other magnet. The arrows appear before contact and remain through the spoken explanation.

narration.title: Matching poles repel
narration.text: Reset the same magnets and turn one around so north faces north. Release from the same gap. They move apart. Repulsion means the magnetic forces push the magnets away from each other. The matched camera view makes the changed pole arrangement clear.

narration.title: Test the effect of distance
narration.text: Keep the magnets, pole arrangement, track and release method the same. Change only the starting gap: one, four, then eight centimetres. Measure how far the moving magnet travels in two seconds, and repeat every gap three times.

narration.title: Read the distance evidence
narration.text: At one centimetre the magnet moves 14 centimetres. At four centimetres it moves 6. At eight centimetres it moves less than 1 in the same time. Greater distance gives a smaller observed effect in this setup.

narration.title: Design a cabinet catch
narration.text: A cabinet catch must pull the door closed before its magnet touches the steel plate. A wide gap gives too little visible movement; a narrow gap works reliably. The design uses attraction across a gap and distance evidence, not a hidden hook.

narration.title: Test every metal
narration.text: Someone claims magnets attract every metal. Test that claim against the labelled samples. Steel moves, while aluminium and copper do not move in the repeated test. One clear counterexample is enough to reject the word every.

narration.title: Use the evidence precisely
narration.text: Replace the claim: magnets attract some materials, including the tested steel. Two magnets may attract or repel depending on which poles face. The observed effect also changes with distance. Keep each conclusion tied to the evidence actually collected.

narration.title: Predict before release
narration.text: Three setups wait at equal gaps: north facing south, north facing north, and north facing aluminium. Predict move together, move apart or no visible movement in this test. For each choice, name the pole or material evidence that supports it.

tests.prompt: Which tested object should an ordinary bar magnet attract across a small gap?
tests.feedback: The repeated test showed the steel paperclip responding while the other listed samples did not.

tests.prompt: Which conclusion fits tests of steel, aluminium, copper and wood?
options: The magnet attracted steel, not every tested metal
The magnet attracted every shiny sample
tests.feedback: Aluminium and copper are metals but did not respond in this setup, so every metal is too broad.

tests.prompt: A paperclip begins moving before the magnet touches it. What does this show?
options: Magnetic force can act across a gap
tests.feedback: Movement beginning with a visible gap is evidence of a non-contact magnetic interaction.

tests.prompt: Why must the gap remain visible in the material demonstration?
options: It shows the motion begins without contact
It proves the object moves because of a hidden push
It ensures all metals respond in the same way
It shows magnetic force begins only after touching
tests.feedback: A visible gap rules out direct contact as the cause of the first movement.

tests.prompt: A north pole faces a south pole. What should happen after release?
options: The magnets move towards each other
Neither magnet can experience a force
tests.feedback: Opposite poles attract, so each magnet is pulled towards the other.

tests.prompt: Which arrow model matches north-south attraction?
options: An arrow on each magnet pointing towards the other
Both arrows pointing the same way
Arrows only after the magnets touch
One downward gravity arrow labelled magnetism
tests.feedback: Attraction pulls both receiving magnets towards one another across the gap.

tests.prompt: Two north poles face at the same gap. What is the best prediction?
options: They move together because all poles attract
They remain still because magnets need contact
Only one magnet moves because only one exerts a force
tests.feedback: Matching poles repel, producing a force on each magnet away from the other.

tests.prompt: Which arrow model matches repulsion between two magnets?
options: An arrow on each magnet pointing away from the other
Both arrows pointing into the gap
No arrows because they do not touch
tests.feedback: Repulsion acts on both magnets and pushes each away from the other.

tests.prompt: Which plan fairly tests the effect of magnet distance?
options: Same magnets and pole arrangement; change only the starting gap
Change magnets, poles and gaps together
Use one gap with different tracks
Push one magnet by hand at each start
tests.feedback: Changing only the starting gap isolates distance as the possible cause of changed motion.

tests.prompt: In the distance test, what should be measured as the outcome?
options: Distance moved in the same time
Pole arrangement kept for each run
Magnet type kept for each run
tests.feedback: Movement distance is the outcome; starting gap is changed while pole arrangement and magnet type are controlled.

tests.prompt: A magnet moves 14 cm from a 1 cm gap, 6 cm from 4 cm, and less than 1 cm from 8 cm. What pattern is supported?
options: The observed effect became smaller as the gap increased
The effect became larger with distance
The magnet stopped being magnetic after one run
tests.feedback: The measured movement decreases as the starting gap increases in this setup.

tests.prompt: Why repeat the 1, 4 and 8 cm gap trials?
options: To check that the distance pattern is consistent
To force every result to match
To prove all magnets behave identically
tests.feedback: Repeats reveal variation and show whether the measured distance pattern is dependable.

tests.prompt: Which evidence directly challenges 'magnets attract every metal'?
options: The labelled aluminium and copper samples do not move
The ruler shows a small gap
tests.feedback: Non-responsive aluminium and copper samples are metal counterexamples to the word every.

tests.prompt: Why is 'magnets attract shiny things' a poor rule?
options: Shine does not predict the tested material response
Every shiny sample should be grouped as steel
Colour is better evidence than repeated movement
One responding shiny sample proves all shiny samples respond
tests.feedback: Material tests, not appearance, showed which samples responded to the magnet.

tests.prompt: Which setup changes only pole arrangement?
options: Same magnets and gap, first north-south then north-north
One magnet on a new track with a hand push
tests.feedback: Keeping magnets and gap fixed isolates which poles face as the planned change.

tests.prompt: Why should pole colours and labels stay fixed in every shot?
options: So attraction and repulsion comparisons cannot be confused
So colour alone creates the force
So magnets attract every red object
tests.feedback: Stable labels make the changed pole arrangement clear and keep the model interpretable.

tests.prompt: A cabinet magnet is too far from its steel plate to pull the door closed reliably. Which change best uses the evidence?
options: Reduce the gap while keeping alignment
Paint the plate a shinier colour
tests.feedback: The tests showed a larger observed effect at smaller gaps, so reducing the gap is evidence-based.

tests.prompt: Which cabinet-catch observation is evidence of magnetic attraction?
options: The steel plate begins moving towards the magnet before contact
The steel plate stays still at every tested gap
The plate moves only after the door directly pushes it
The plate drops towards Earth when detached
tests.feedback: Motion towards the magnet across a visible gap is evidence of attraction rather than direct contact or gravity.

tests.prompt: At equal gaps, what should happen for north-south, north-north and north-aluminium?
options: Together, apart, no visible movement in this test
tests.feedback: Opposite poles attract, matching poles repel, and the tested aluminium sample did not respond.

tests.prompt: Which conclusion uses material, pole and distance evidence precisely?
options: The tested steel responds; pole arrangement sets attraction or repulsion; the observed effect decreases with gap
Every metal is attracted equally at every distance
Pole arrangement matters only after contact
Distance changes which material an object is
tests.feedback: The conclusion matches all three investigations without claiming more than their evidence supports.

chapters.title: Forces Team Up
chapters.learningOutcome: Use several qualitative arrows to predict motion.

chapters.title: Air Pushes Back
chapters.learningOutcome: Investigate how shape changes air resistance.

chapters.title: Machines Trade Force For Distance
chapters.learningOutcome: Explain how ramps and levers trade force for distance.

chapters.title: The Broken Experiment
chapters.learningOutcome: Diagnose unfair tests and strengthen conclusions.

chapters.title: Rescue The Rover
chapters.learningOutcome: Use force evidence to choose and justify an engineering solution.
